title: Setup: R and RStudio
text:
1. Install R

Windows

Go to https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/.

Download “Download R-x.x.x for Windows”.

Run the installer.

Accept the default install location (usually C:\Program Files\R\...).

You can leave the 32-bit option unchecked (64-bit only is fine).


Finish the installer.

Strongly recommended on Windows — Rtools (needed if a package must compile from source, e.g. some updates of xgboost or glmnet):

Go to https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/.

Install the Rtools version that matches your R version (the page explains which).

Use the default options so Rtools is on the system PATH.

Without Rtools, many packages still install as pre-built binaries. If install fails with messages about g++, make, or “compilation failed,” install Rtools and try again.


macOS

Go to https://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/.

Download the installer for your chip:

Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4): usually labeled arm64

Intel: usually labeled x86_64


To check your chip: Apple menu → About This Mac.

Open the .pkg and complete installation.

If macOS blocks the installer: System Settings → Privacy & Security → allow the app, or right-click → Open.



Linux
Use your distribution’s instructions on CRAN, or install from https://cran.r-project.org/ for your distro. On Ubuntu/Debian you typically need build tools (build-essential) for source packages.


Quick check
In RStudio later, run:
R.version.string
You should see a recent version (4.3+ preferred).

title: Setup: R and RStudio
text:
2. Install RStudio Desktop (Posit)
All systems:

Go to https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/.

Download RStudio Desktop Free for your OS.

Install and open RStudio.

Confirm the Console shows an R version and a > prompt.


Windows tips

Install R before RStudio.

If RStudio says it cannot find R:
Tools → Global Options → General → R version → Change and point to your R install under C:\Program Files\R\.

Prefer installing to a path without unusual characters. Default paths are fine.

Run RStudio as a normal user for daily work (not always “as Administrator”).



macOS tips

Drag RStudio into Applications.

First launch: right-click → Open if Gatekeeper blocks it.

If you have both Intel and ARM R, keep one clear default.

You will do almost all course work in RStudio: open .qmd files, run code chunks, and Knit/Render when asked.

title: Setup: R and RStudio
text:
3. Install Quarto (recommended)
Quarto powers our lecture notes and labs (.qmd files).

Go to https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/.

Install Quarto for Windows / macOS / Linux.

Fully quit and reopen RStudio after installing.


Check

Windows: open Command Prompt or PowerShell (not only R):
quarto --version

macOS / Linux: Terminal:
quarto --version

If this fails but RStudio still runs code chunks, you can work day-to-day; full website/render features may need Quarto fixed. Ask me early if quarto is not found after install (Windows PATH issues are common—restart the PC once after installing Quarto).

title: Setup: R and RStudio
text:
4. Install course packages

4.1 Easiest method

Download install-packages.R from this Setup page (or copy from the course site).

In RStudio: File → Open File → select install-packages.R.

Click Source, or run:

source("install-packages.R", echo = TRUE)
(Adjust the path if the file is in Downloads, e.g. on Windows: source("C:/Users/YourName/Downloads/install-packages.R").)


4.2 Or paste this in the RStudio console
This can take 10–30 minutes. Stay online.

# Prefer binaries when possible (especially Windows)
options(install.packages.check.source = "no")
options(pkgType = ifelse(.Platform$OS.type == "windows", "binary", getOption("pkgType")))

# --- CORE (required for most of the course) ---
core <- c(
  "tidyverse",     # data wrangling + ggplot2
  "scales",
  "tidymodels",    # modeling workflow
  "glmnet",        # ridge / lasso
  "rpart",         # decision trees
  "rpart.plot",
  "ranger",        # random forests
  "vip",
  "cluster",
  "factoextra",
  "ggfortify",
  "pROC",          # ROC / AUC
  "nnet",          # simple neural nets (intro)
  "rmarkdown",
  "knitr",
  "gt",
  "broom",
  "here"
)

# --- RECOMMENDED (used later; install now if you can) ---
recommended <- c(
  "xgboost"        # boosting — sometimes needs Rtools on Windows
)

install_set <- function(pkgs) {
  missing <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% rownames(installed.packages())]
  if (!length(missing)) {
    message("Already installed: ", paste(pkgs, collapse = ", "))
    return(invisible(TRUE))
  }
  message("Installing: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
  for (p in missing) {
    message("--> ", p)
    tryCatch(
      install.packages(p, dependencies = TRUE),
      error = function(e) message("FAILED: ", p, " — ", conditionMessage(e))
    )
  }
}

install_set(core)
install_set(recommended)

# Report status
all_pkgs <- c(core, recommended)
ok <- vapply(all_pkgs, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE, FUN.VALUE = logical(1))
print(ok)
if (!all(ok[core])) {
  stop("Core packages still missing: ", paste(names(ok[core])[!ok[core]], collapse = ", "))
}
if (!ok["xgboost"]) {
  message("NOTE: xgboost failed. You can still start the course; we will revisit before boosting week. On Windows, install Rtools and retry.")
} else {
  message("All core + recommended packages look good.")
}



4.3 Optional later (do not block Week 1)
Only if we announce them for neural-net / API demos:

# install.packages("torch")   # heavy; Windows/macOS have specific install docs
# install.packages("luz")
# install.packages(c("httr2", "jsonlite"))

title: Setup: R and RStudio
text:
5. Verify your setup (must pass)
Run in the RStudio console—no red errors:

need <- c(
  "tidyverse", "tidymodels", "glmnet", "rpart", "ranger",
  "cluster", "pROC", "nnet", "broom", "here"
)

ok <- vapply(need, requireNamespace, quietly = TRUE, FUN.VALUE = logical(1))
print(ok)

if (!all(ok)) {
  stop("Missing packages: ", paste(names(ok)[!ok], collapse = ", "))
} else {
  message("Core packages OK.")
}

# Smoke test: tiny linear model
library(tidymodels)
set.seed(467)
dat <- data.frame(x = rnorm(50), y = NA_real_)
dat$y <- 1 + 2 * dat$x + rnorm(50)
fit <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm") |> fit(y ~ x, data = dat)
print(broom::tidy(fit))
message("Smoke test passed — modeling stack works.")

You should see a small table of coefficients (intercept and x).

Problem

title: 70-467 - Machine Learning for Business Analytics
text:
CMU-Q · Fall 2026 · 70-467




Instructor: Andrés Castaño Zuluaga


Welcome to 70-467 Machine Learning for Business Analytics!


In an era when AI can write code faster than most people, writing code is not the scarce skill. The bottleneck in productive analytics is understanding, verification, and judgment: knowing what to ask the tools to do, checking whether the answer is good enough to act on, and explaining both the recommendation and its limits. AI will not replace your job. Someone who can use it and is prepared to work those bottlenecks will.
This course prepares you for that. You cannot evaluate the tools, or incorporate them into how you work, until you understand the methods. That is what sharpens judgment and makes the communication defensible. We incentivize responsible use of AI: tools that augment you, not substitutes that replace the thinking. You will learn to turn data into decisions you can stand behind. Choose the method, check it carefully, and explain the recommendation and its limits. The emphasis is business judgment under real problems, not model fitting as an end in itself. We work in R, with real datasets.


Mon & Wed · 2:30–3:45 PM · CMB 1190 Concepts + R labs

title: 70-467 - Machine Learning for Business Analytics
section: Methods you will see and use
text:
Methods you will see and use
We move from simple, interpretable models to richer tools, always starting from a business problem and emphasizing business understanding, method feasibility and limitations, and judgement in decision-making.

  
    
    Linear regression
    Quantitative outcomes; the workhorse we start with
  
  
    
    Logistic regression
    Classification when the outcome is a category
  
  
    
    Trees and ensembles
    CART, random forests, boosting
  
  
    
    PCA
    Reducing dimensions when you have many variables
  
  
    
    Clustering
    Grouping without a pre-labeled outcome
  
  
    
    Neural nets
    A short look, late in the term, if time allows
  

Full week-by-week plan: Schedule.

title: 70-467 - Machine Learning for Business Analytics
text:
How we work
A simple weekly rhythm so you always know how to prepare.

  
    
      
    
    01 · Before class
    Lecture notes
    Read the assigned textbook sections and, when assigned, run the Quarto notes. Those notes are in Quarto, so complete the setup instructions early. You need a working machine for the week to week flow of the course.
  
  
    
      
    
    02 · Monday
    Concepts & decisions
     Mondays are for understanding the method, always starting from a business problem. You prepare a short introduction to that method and present it. I then take over and finish the lecture. The presentation schedule comes in week two, once enrollment is set.
  
  
    
      
    
    03 · Wednesday
    R lab
    Wednesdays are labs, and we start from a problem, not from the code. The problem is posted before class. Come prepared. In class we work through guided notebooks: some of the code is already there, you complete the TODOs, we run it, and we interpret the output together. Then we argue the merits of the analysis and how to make it stronger.
  
  
    
      
    
    04 · Outside class
    Build and defend
    For homework you get real data, a problem, and starter code. You turn in a notebook, at most six slides, and a video of at most five minutes — same story in all three. The project is individual and ends with an in-class presentation; details are in the syllabus.

title: 70-467 — Machine Learning for Business Analytics
text:
Course Description
Organizations that turn data into good decisions need people who can do more than just run scripts in a given software or use AI to do the job for them. They need analysts who can start from a business problem, choose an appropriate method, evaluate a model honestly, interpret the result carefully, and recommend an action, including what the model cannot do.
This course introduces the core machine learning tools used in modern business analytics, with applications from marketing, finance, operations, and related areas. You will implement methods in R, work from real-world datasets, and practice professional communication through slide decks, recorded presentations, and an individual project presented in class at the end of the course. The course prepares you for consulting and analytics-oriented roles in finance, operations, marketing, and similar fields.
Because generative AI is now part of how technical work gets done, you will also learn how to use it to improve your understanding of the methods and their software implementation, while remaining responsible for verification, judgment, and academic integrity.
Prerequisites: Statistics (70-207 or 36-200 or 36-220 or equivalent). Comfort with R and basic regression is expected. Prior machine learning is not required.

title: 70-467 — Machine Learning for Business Analytics
text:
Learning Objectives
On completing the course, you should be able to:

Build analytics models using R and use them for business decision-making.
Translate a data-driven business problem into analytical models based on its purpose, available data, solution methods, evaluation metrics, and business decision-making.
Exercise judgment when choosing among supervised and unsupervised methods, model families, features, validation strategies, and regularization techniques, always letting the problem and the data determine the choice rather than habit.
Communicate the results of technical business data analysis models to a business audience to convince them of its value, validity, effectiveness, and potential limitations.
Learn how to use AI effectively to improve your coding skills and to augment the quality of your work in translating data-driven business problems into analytical models and business decisions.

title: 70-467 — Machine Learning for Business Analytics
text:
Course Materials
The main readings will be based on suggested readings from the main textbook, along with my notes. I write those notes from the parts of ISLR that we actually use that week, and I add the pieces ISLR does not cover. I will post class slides PDFs on the course website and Canvas after class.

[ISLR] James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani. An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R (2nd ed.). The book is free online. The notes will point you to the sections we used in class.
Additional notes and readings will be posted on the website and Canvas as needed. Check that you can open the materials and let me know if something does not work.
We will use R and RStudio (Posit). Labs and homeworks start from scripts I provide: your job is to understand them, interpret the results, and modify them based on the problem at hand. Bring a laptop to every lab.
There is a setup page on the website with the packages to install. Please do this before the first lab and email me if something doesn’t work, so we can use lab time for methods rather than troubleshooting installation. Make sure you do this after the first class and reach out if there are issues to solve.

title: 70-467 — Machine Learning for Business Analytics
text:
Delivery of Lectures and Labs
Our lectures and labs are in person. They will not be recorded. A typical week looks like this:

Monday: Most weeks, a student pair opens with a short presentation introducing the method through a business problem. I then continue with the discussion and the details (formulas, short code, and interpretation).
Wednesday: Lab in R. You will get the problem before class and a starter notebook with parts already working. In the hour we work on approach, interpretation, figures, and what the results mean for the decision.

Assessment Descriptions
Homeworks. There will be four individual homeworks. Each one is a new case using the methods we have covered, not a repeat of the lab. I will give you a case, the data, a codebook, and starter code. You submit three pieces on Canvas: a runnable R notebook, at most six slides, and a video of at most five minutes. The slides and the video should tell the same story as the notebook: the problem, the evidence, the decision, and the limit. More details about the expectations will be available on Canvas.
You may study with classmates. The write-up, the code you submit, and the recommendation have to be yours. AI is allowed on homework if you disclose it (see below). You must run the code and be able to explain the important parts of how you reached the decision. If you hide AI use, or you cannot explain the work in the video, or I suspect you used AI inappropriately, I will ask you to present in person. Depending on how you handle the questions in person, the grade on that homework can go as low as 0, and you may be reported for an academic integrity violation.
Quizzes. There will be four short in-class paper quizzes, designed for about 10–15 minutes. They test whether you understand the ideas and can apply the methods to understand and make business decisions. There is no make-up for quizzes.
Pair presentations. Because this is a small class, participation matters. Student pairs will prepare a short presentation (about 8–10 minutes, compact slide deck) at least twice in the semester to introduce that week’s topic. We will then transition into a lecture about the method and the empirical implementation. The rubric will be on the course site / Canvas. The official pairing will be set once we know with certainty how many students are in the course.
The midterm will be in person during class on Wednesday 7 October (75 minutes). Closed notes. No electronic devices. The exam covers weeks 1–5 only: linear regression, metrics, train/test and generalization, regularization, and cross-validation/model selection.
Final project. The final project is an individual project. It’s based on a business problem coming from a real-world dataset. The student will then build models in R to better understand the problem, present a recommendation, and discuss the decisions in an in-class presentation at the end of the semester. I will publish the project brief (including data and problem options once they are ready) by 28 October. I will share exact instructions for what’s expected at checkpoint 1 and during the final presentations later in the semester. Presentations are 30 November and 2 December.
Attendance and participation are part of the grading and will be combined. Please come to each class ready to participate in the discussion of the material or bring questions that could benefit the rest of the group. By mid-semester, I will share your participation and attendance grades, so you have time to adjust appropriately during the second part of the semester, if needed.
How will attendance and participation be graded? If you have various excused or unexcused absences, that counts toward limited participation because you need to be in the classroom to participate. Similarly, if you attend all the classes but rarely participate during class, don’t expect your grade to be solely based on attendance. Finally, if you arrive to class early, but leave the classroom for long periods, don’t expect your grade to be based on arriving on time. I acknowledge that grading participation could be subjective. Still, I will do my best to evaluate students not only on quantity but also on the quality of their participation.


Final grades
Final grades are based on your cumulative score using the weights above. Students with 90–100% receive an A; 80–89% a B; 70–79% a C; 60–69% a D; below 60% an R.
A quick note on calculating your cumulative score: Please use the weights in the table above. I compute the course grade from those weights. Canvas is not always reliable here. If Canvas and that calculation disagree, email me.
In the interests of fairness, we apply the same rules to everyone. Therefore, we cannot modify the cumulative score formula or offer extra work to raise your grade to accommodate your circumstances. The only exception is for midterms missed due to documented illness or a family emergency. Some students will inevitably fall close to, but below, a cutoff when we assign grades. Such students sometimes ask for cutoffs to be reduced. Please do not do this. If you are just below a cutoff, you may be close to the lowest A or B but still some way from the average A or B, and we consider these when assigning cutoffs.

QBA Classroom Conduct — Fall 2026
The Qatar Business Administration Program maintains high expectations for student classroom conduct. Your professors will hold you to these standards. We believe these standards create an environment most conducive to learning. This behavior also reflects common business culture. As CMU Qatar Business Administration students, part of your business education is to model the behavior that you will demonstrate in the workplace.
QBA students attend all scheduled classes. Unless I explicitly state that another way of completing the work is acceptable, you must attend. If you cannot attend, contact me in advance when possible, and as soon as possible if not. You are responsible for obtaining notes and materials.
QBA students attend class on time. Be in class before 2:30 pm. I reserve the right to deny late admission to avoid disrupting the session.
QBA students remain in class once it has begun. Leaving in the middle disrupts peers and presenters. During quizzes and the midterm, you may not be allowed to reenter if you leave.
QBA students come to class prepared. Complete the lecture notes before class. On lab days, read the problem before you sit down. Bring a laptop to labs.
QBA students use electronics only for class purposes. On Mondays, laptops are closed unless I ask you to open them for a short demonstration. On Wednesdays, laptops are required for R. Phones are silent and put away. Do not check email, message, or browse during class.
QBA students adhere to the CMU Policy on Academic Integrity. Representing someone else’s work as your own, or helping someone else to do so, violates academic integrity. Copying a classmate’s notebook, using a past year’s submission, or taking credit for a partner’s pair talk while contributing nothing are examples. Sharing unauthorized answer keys is unauthorized assistance for both parties. I determine what is appropriate in this course; if you are unsure, ask before you act.
Please see CMU’s policies on cheating and plagiarism:
https://www.cmu.edu/policies/student-and-student-life/academic-integrity.html
If you are under pressure, talk to me early. There is almost always a better path than a bad decision. Your academic and behavioral responsibilities are detailed in the Q-Word Student Handbook and the CMU Undergraduate Catalog.

Use of Generative AI Tools
Certain assignments in this course will permit or even encourage the use of AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, and others, to improve your coding and understanding. When AI use is allowed, it will be clearly stated in the assignment. Otherwise, AI is not allowed by default.
When AI is allowed, you must acknowledge how you used it. For instance: “I used Gemini to debug an error in my glmnet call and edited the code for correctness.” You are responsible for assessing whether the output is valid. You may not earn full credit if inaccurate or invalid information is found in your work. Misrepresenting AI use is an academic integrity violation. Expectations differ across courses; email me if you are unsure what is allowed on a given assignment.
Two ways to think about the use of AI in this course. Depending on the assignment, AI is accepted with caution or not allowed.

Yellow level: AI with caution
Homework and the project (when the assignment allows it). You may use AI to learn, debug, and clarify concepts. The analysis, interpretation, and recommendation must be yours. You must run the code, understand the results, and make sure the figures in the video match the notebook.
